questions.stem: Bipartite Matching reduces to max-flow on a network where edges have capacity:
choices: 1 on every edge (s-edges, middle edges, t-edges)
Equal to the number of neighbours
questions.explanation: Unit capacities ensure each L-vertex and R-vertex is matched at most once and let integrality produce a combinatorial matching.

questions.stem: What is the running time of Edmonds-Karp?
questions.explanation: BFS for shortest augmenting paths gives O(mn) augmentations * O(m) per augmentation = O(m^2 n).

questions.stem: Why is integrality crucial for max-flow-as-reduction?
choices: It ensures the algorithmic output corresponds to a combinatorial solution (0/1 selections)
questions.explanation: Fractional flows in the original network would not decode to discrete combinatorial objects (matchings, paths). Integrality gives a clean decoding.

questions.stem: Konig's theorem says, in bipartite graphs:
questions.explanation: Konig's theorem is the bipartite case of LP duality; it follows from MFMC on the matching network.

questions.stem: Menger's theorem (edge version) states:
choices: Max # edge-disjoint s-t paths = min # edges whose removal disconnects s from t
Max flow value = sum of capacities
All graphs have an Eulerian path
questions.explanation: Menger follows from MFMC with unit-capacity edges: max-flow = max edge-disjoint paths = min edge cut.

questions.stem: Image segmentation is reduced to:
questions.explanation: The MIN s-t cut separates foreground (A side) from background (B side); a constant offset turns the MAX likelihood into a MIN cost.

questions.stem: How is multi-source max-flow reduced to standard single-source/single-sink?
choices: Add a super-source connected to each original source with capacity = supply
Run the algorithm on each source independently
questions.explanation: Standard trick: super-source / super-sink with supply / demand capacities; symmetric for multi-sink.

questions.stem: What is capacity scaling's main advantage?
choices: Works for irrational capacities (Edmonds-Karp already does)
Runtime is O(m^2 log C), better than O(m^2 n) when C is small
It is exact only in expectation
questions.explanation: Capacity scaling phases by halving threshold Delta give O(m^2 log C); useful when max capacity C is large but path counts are small.

questions.stem: After computing max bipartite matching as max-flow, the matching is read off by:
questions.explanation: Middle edges saturated by integer flow are exactly the matched pairs.

questions.stem: Why do both directions of the reduction equivalence need to be proved?
choices: To show OBJECTIVE(I) = MAXFLOW(G'); inequality in one direction alone is insufficient
questions.explanation: Forward (solution -> flow) shows MAXFLOW >= OBJ; backward (flow -> solution) shows OBJ >= MAXFLOW. Together they give equality.

questions.stem: How would you reduce 'max number of vertex-disjoint s-t paths' to max-flow?
choices: Split each internal vertex v into v_in -> v_out with capacity 1 internal edge; capacity 1 on original edges
questions.explanation: Node-splitting transforms vertex-capacity 1 into edge-capacity 1 inside the constructed network.

questions.stem: Bipartite Matching reduction's max-flow runtime is bounded by:
questions.explanation: Ford-Fulkerson finds at most min(|L|, |R|) augmentations (max matching size), each O(m). With unit capacities this is tight.

questions.stem: In the image segmentation network, neighbouring-pixel penalties p_{ij} appear as:
choices: Two anti-parallel edges (i, j) and (j, i), each of capacity p_{ij}
questions.explanation: Anti-parallel pair so that whichever side i and j end up on, exactly one direction contributes p_{ij} to the cut.

questions.stem: Which problem CANNOT be modelled as polynomial-size max-flow?
questions.explanation: TSP is NP-hard and has no known polynomial reduction to max-flow. The others all do.

questions.stem: Baseball elimination uses max-flow to determine:
choices: Whether team z is mathematically already eliminated
questions.explanation: Team z is eliminated iff max-flow in the constructed network < total remaining games, meaning some game outcomes are infeasible.

questions.stem: After Edmonds-Karp terminates, the min cut is:
choices: {vertices reachable from s in G_f} vs rest
questions.explanation: Same as standard Ford-Fulkerson — A = reachable set from s in G_f decodes the min cut.

questions.stem: Which is FALSE about Edmonds-Karp?
choices: It uses BFS to find augmenting paths
It is a strongly polynomial algorithm
Each augmentation increases path length monotonically
questions.explanation: Edmonds-Karp's O(m^2 n) bound does NOT depend on capacities — it is strongly polynomial.

questions.stem: In a unit-capacity network, max-flow equals:
questions.explanation: By Menger / integrality, unit-capacity max-flow decomposes into that many edge-disjoint paths.

questions.stem: What does the cut in the image-segmentation min-cut decode into?
choices: The labelling of pixels as foreground (s-side) or background (t-side)
A list of edges to remove
questions.explanation: Vertices on the s-side = foreground; t-side = background. Cut capacity = total penalty + unchosen likelihoods.

questions.stem: Why use a super-source/super-sink in matching, instead of treating each L-vertex as a source?
choices: It collapses multi-source/multi-sink into single-source/single-sink, so standard Ford-Fulkerson applies
questions.explanation: Single-source / single-sink is the standard max-flow setting; the super-source / super-sink trick is the universal way to reduce.

questions.stem: In a bipartite matching reduction, what does a fractional max-flow of value 2.5 imply?
choices: It cannot happen with integer capacities
questions.explanation: Integer capacities + Ford-Fulkerson => integer flow. A fractional value is impossible in this setting.

questions.stem: Which capacity choice would make the bipartite matching reduction INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: Capacity 2 on s-edges would let one L-vertex be 'matched' to two R-vertices, breaking the matching constraint.

questions.stem: Network construction time for these reductions is usually:
questions.explanation: All reductions in Week 7 build a network of size polynomial (typically linear) in input size. Required for the overall algorithm to be polynomial.

questions.stem: What is the typical way to convert a MAX objective into a min-cut formulation (e.g., image segmentation)?
choices: Subtract the MAX objective from a problem-specific constant; what was max becomes min
questions.explanation: Image segmentation expresses sum of likelihoods plus a constant offset, turning MAX likelihood into MIN of the cut capacity.

questions.stem: Which is the safest exam strategy when given a problem that 'feels like' it might reduce to max-flow?
choices: Identify nodes (entities), edges (constraints), capacities (limits), and check whether unit / integer capacities give the desired combinatorial decoding
questions.explanation: Disciplined reduction design: list entities, capture constraints as edges with capacities, then check integrality and decoding.
